analysis.one_liner: Stops companies from using bankruptcy to cap liability for mass injury lawsuits.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by a bipartisan trio of senators, was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee in July 2024 and never received a vote before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill targets a bankruptcy tactic used by large companies facing thousands of injury lawsuits, such as talc and asbestos claims. A company would split off the liabilities into a new subsidiary and file for Chapter 11, using the automatic stay to freeze lawsuits against the parent company and managers, then ask a bankruptcy judge to cap the total payout. Under this bill, a bankruptcy filing that exists mainly to dodge or cap those lawsuits could be thrown out as made in bad faith, and the automatic stay would no longer shield parent companies, officers, and insurers from suits on claims affecting 100 or more people.
analysis.who_benefits: People injured by a company's product, material, or contamination, and other creditors, who would again be able to sue the parent companies, officers, and insurers behind the bankrupt entity instead of being funneled into a court-ordered settlement with a fixed total payout.

how_it_helps.text: A bankruptcy judge would have to dismiss a Chapter 11 case whose filing or continuation is objectively futile or in subjective bad faith, shifting the burden of proof to the company.

A filing would be conclusively presumed bad faith if its purpose or effect is to cap the debtor's total liability to creditors holding protected claims the company could pay in full, to gain a litigation advantage, or to delay creditors, or if the company lacks any valid purpose of reorganizing.
A bankruptcy court would presume bad faith when a company manufactured the court's venue, rebuttable only by clear and convincing evidence, targeting forum shopping into debtor-friendly courts.

The automatic stay, which normally freezes all collection and lawsuit activity, would no longer apply to lawsuits against non-debtor entities, such as parent companies, officers, directors, and insurers, on claims affecting at least 100 people arising from exposure to a product or substance, when the company went through a divisional merger, spinoff, or restructuring in the previous four years.
Bankruptcy courts could no longer issue orders that override this limitation on the automatic stay, closing the route by which bankruptcy judges have barred suits against non-debtor companies.

analysis.who_pays: Large companies facing mass injury litigation, their parent companies and private equity owners, their officers and directors, and the insurers that cover them, which would lose the ability to confine liability to a bankruptcy settlement with a fixed cap.

drawbacks.text: Companies facing genuine mass liabilities argue that a single bankruptcy proceeding can compensate claimants more evenly and completely than thousands of separate lawsuits, which can exhaust assets unevenly and leave late claimants unpaid; this bill narrows that channel.

The bill applies to any case filed or pending on or after enactment, and its conclusive presumptions, such as one triggered by any divisional merger or restructuring in the prior four years, could sweep in legitimate reorganizations and push distressed companies toward liquidation rather than reorganization, costing jobs and reducing total recoveries for creditors and claimants.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people with injury claims against companies that split off liabilities and filed bankruptcy to cap them, the bill restores a meaningful path to full compensation, at a real cost to orderly resolution for the minority of distressed companies using bankruptcy legitimately. The bill tries to separate the two by conditioning its harshest provisions on recent restructuring maneuvers and on filings lacking a genuine reorganizational purpose, but the conclusive presumptions and retroactive application risk catching legitimate cases.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee in July 2024, and it never received a committee vote or floor action before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse introduced the bill on July 23, 2024, joined by original cosponsors Sens. Josh Hawley and Richard Durbin.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day.
No further action, committee markup, or vote appears in the bill's action history, and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, so the bill died in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies facing mass injury lawsuits keep the option of capping their liabilities through a strategically filed bankruptcy, including forum shopping into favorable courts, because no law changed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Companies capping tort liabilities via bankruptcy

sides.party_line_note: The bill's three named supporters split across party lines, a Democrat sponsoring and one Democrat and one Republican cosponsoring, and no opposition appears in the record; the bill simply died in committee without a vote.

industries.note: These companies use Chapter 11 filings, often after splitting off liabilities, to freeze lawsuits and cap total payouts to injury claimants. The bill would let courts dismiss such filings as bad faith and lift the stay protecting their parents and officers, restoring claimants' ability to pursue full payment.

industries.industry: Private equity and corporate parents of bankrupt subsidiaries
industries.note: Owners commonly restructure a business into separate entities before bankruptcy so the profitable parent stays shielded while the liabilities land in the filing. The bill removes the automatic stay's protection for these non-debtor owners on claims affecting 100 or more people.

Insurers that provided coverage to the debtor count as protected-claim targets under the bill, so suits against them could no longer be stayed out of the bankruptcy. Insurers would face direct claims that bankruptcy filings currently freeze.
A large share of complex Chapter 11 work depends on mass-tort cases filed to manage liabilities. Fewer such filings would reduce that business, while legitimate restructurings continue.
